async function fetch(url) {
  const { packId, path } = manifest.lookup(url)
  const pack = await memo(packCache, packId, async () => {

    return decode(await response.blob())
  })

  return new Response(await pack.text(path))
}

Reading the totals

Start with Comparable request window. This is the closest asset-level wall-clock comparison because it collapses overlapping request waits into a union: TP 1633 ms, comparable baseline 4546 ms.

Do not read diagnostic sums as page duration. Values like TP 13196 ms or baseline 63557 ms are sums across many overlapping rows. They are useful for finding where work accumulated, but they are not directly comparable to the top-level load time.

TP work breakdown = sum of unique pack/file fetch work + per-asset extract + per-asset overhead across served-from-pack assets = 706 ms + 12312 ms + 178 ms = 13196 ms
Excluded duplicated waits: 27219 ms. Raw paused sum before excluding waits: 40415 ms.

TP effective asset sum = TP work breakdown + sum of baseline-fetch ms for assets TP fell through on
= 13196 ms + 0 ms (0 fall-throughs paid network cost) = 13196 ms

Comparable baseline diagnostic sum = baseline fetch sum for rows TP served = 63557 ms
All observed BL asset wait sum = 76339 ms

Reading this table

  • Pack/file fetch+decode — full/stream variants show the time this request waited for pack initialization. Range-stream variants show metadata wait plus file-region fetch wait. miss is the first initializer for a pack, pending means this asset arrived while another request was already initializing the same pack, and hit means metadata/decode was already available at request start.
  • Baseline asset fetch — time to fetch this single asset over the wire in baseline mode. Adjacent for direct comparison.
  • Extract — pack.extract(file), in-memory, sub-millisecond.
  • SW overhead — total − fetch − extract. Browser-side Service Worker response construction and marker-message overhead. No Playwright/CDP fulfill path is included.
  • TokenPack total — fetch + extract + overhead. The wall-clock time spent producing this asset response.
  • Green/red coloring compares real work (fetch + extract) vs baseline fetch — i.e., what TokenPack would cost without the harness tax. Green on the TokenPack side = real work was faster than the baseline fetch.
  • outside TP manifest — baseline fetched this URL, but it is outside the comparable manifest-handled URL set for this sampled phase. This is not a TokenPack miss.
  • TP did not request — baseline fetched this comparable manifest URL, but the TokenPack run did not request it in the sampled phase. A large cluster usually means the TP page diverged or failed before reaching that import path; an isolated row can also come from feature flags, lazy imports, version drift, or conditional app flow.
  • TP-only (not in BL) — TokenPack requested this URL but baseline never did. Different code path got executed (feature flag, A/B variant, error-recovery branch).

Column sums overstate wall-clock because requests run in parallel. Iteration durations are the real answer.

Reading the totals

Start with Comparable request window. This is the closest asset-level wall-clock comparison because it collapses overlapping request waits into a union: TP 450 ms, comparable baseline 5330 ms.

Do not read diagnostic sums as page duration. Values like TP 450 ms or baseline 50060 ms are sums across many overlapping rows. They are useful for finding where work accumulated, but they are not directly comparable to the top-level load time.

TP work breakdown = sum of unique pack/file fetch work + per-asset extract + per-asset overhead across served-from-pack assets = 0 ms + 449 ms + 1 ms = 450 ms
Excluded duplicated waits: 1 ms. Raw paused sum before excluding waits: 450 ms.

TP effective asset sum = TP work breakdown + sum of baseline-fetch ms for assets TP fell through on
= 450 ms + 0 ms (0 fall-throughs paid network cost) = 450 ms

Comparable baseline diagnostic sum = baseline fetch sum for rows TP served = 50060 ms
All observed BL asset wait sum = 73969 ms

Reading this table

  • Pack/file fetch+decode — full/stream variants show the time this request waited for pack initialization. Range-stream variants show metadata wait plus file-region fetch wait. miss is the first initializer for a pack, pending means this asset arrived while another request was already initializing the same pack, and hit means metadata/decode was already available at request start.
  • Baseline asset fetch — time to fetch this single asset over the wire in baseline mode. Adjacent for direct comparison.
  • Extract — pack.extract(file), in-memory, sub-millisecond.
  • SW overhead — total − fetch − extract. Browser-side Service Worker response construction and marker-message overhead. No Playwright/CDP fulfill path is included.
  • TokenPack total — fetch + extract + overhead. The wall-clock time spent producing this asset response.
  • Green/red coloring compares real work (fetch + extract) vs baseline fetch — i.e., what TokenPack would cost without the harness tax. Green on the TokenPack side = real work was faster than the baseline fetch.
  • outside TP manifest — baseline fetched this URL, but it is outside the comparable manifest-handled URL set for this sampled phase. This is not a TokenPack miss.
  • TP did not request — baseline fetched this comparable manifest URL, but the TokenPack run did not request it in the sampled phase. A large cluster usually means the TP page diverged or failed before reaching that import path; an isolated row can also come from feature flags, lazy imports, version drift, or conditional app flow.
  • TP-only (not in BL) — TokenPack requested this URL but baseline never did. Different code path got executed (feature flag, A/B variant, error-recovery branch).

Column sums overstate wall-clock because requests run in parallel. Iteration durations are the real answer.

const packCache = new Map()

async function fetch(url) {
  const { packId, path } = manifest.lookup(url)
  const pack = await memo(packCache, packId, async () => {
    const response = await nativeFetch(packUrl(packId))
    return decodeStream(response.body)
  })

  return new Response(await pack.text(path))
}

Reading the totals

Start with Comparable request window. This is the closest asset-level wall-clock comparison because it collapses overlapping request waits into a union: TP 1551 ms, comparable baseline 4546 ms.

Do not read diagnostic sums as page duration. Values like TP 12817 ms or baseline 63557 ms are sums across many overlapping rows. They are useful for finding where work accumulated, but they are not directly comparable to the top-level load time.

TP work breakdown = sum of unique pack/file fetch work + per-asset extract + per-asset overhead across served-from-pack assets = 634 ms + 11980 ms + 203 ms = 12817 ms
Excluded duplicated waits: 14602 ms. Raw paused sum before excluding waits: 27419 ms.

TP effective asset sum = TP work breakdown + sum of baseline-fetch ms for assets TP fell through on
= 12817 ms + 0 ms (0 fall-throughs paid network cost) = 12817 ms

Comparable baseline diagnostic sum = baseline fetch sum for rows TP served = 63557 ms
All observed BL asset wait sum = 76339 ms

Reading this table

  • Pack/file fetch+decode — full/stream variants show the time this request waited for pack initialization. Range-stream variants show metadata wait plus file-region fetch wait. miss is the first initializer for a pack, pending means this asset arrived while another request was already initializing the same pack, and hit means metadata/decode was already available at request start.
  • Baseline asset fetch — time to fetch this single asset over the wire in baseline mode. Adjacent for direct comparison.
  • Extract — pack.extract(file), in-memory, sub-millisecond.
  • SW overhead — total − fetch − extract. Browser-side Service Worker response construction and marker-message overhead. No Playwright/CDP fulfill path is included.
  • TokenPack total — fetch + extract + overhead. The wall-clock time spent producing this asset response.
  • Green/red coloring compares real work (fetch + extract) vs baseline fetch — i.e., what TokenPack would cost without the harness tax. Green on the TokenPack side = real work was faster than the baseline fetch.
  • outside TP manifest — baseline fetched this URL, but it is outside the comparable manifest-handled URL set for this sampled phase. This is not a TokenPack miss.
  • TP did not request — baseline fetched this comparable manifest URL, but the TokenPack run did not request it in the sampled phase. A large cluster usually means the TP page diverged or failed before reaching that import path; an isolated row can also come from feature flags, lazy imports, version drift, or conditional app flow.
  • TP-only (not in BL) — TokenPack requested this URL but baseline never did. Different code path got executed (feature flag, A/B variant, error-recovery branch).

Column sums overstate wall-clock because requests run in parallel. Iteration durations are the real answer.

Reading the totals

Start with Comparable request window. This is the closest asset-level wall-clock comparison because it collapses overlapping request waits into a union: TP 458 ms, comparable baseline 5330 ms.

Do not read diagnostic sums as page duration. Values like TP 456 ms or baseline 50060 ms are sums across many overlapping rows. They are useful for finding where work accumulated, but they are not directly comparable to the top-level load time.

TP work breakdown = sum of unique pack/file fetch work + per-asset extract + per-asset overhead across served-from-pack assets = 0 ms + 453 ms + 3 ms = 456 ms
Excluded duplicated waits: 2 ms. Raw paused sum before excluding waits: 458 ms.

TP effective asset sum = TP work breakdown + sum of baseline-fetch ms for assets TP fell through on
= 456 ms + 0 ms (0 fall-throughs paid network cost) = 456 ms

Comparable baseline diagnostic sum = baseline fetch sum for rows TP served = 50060 ms
All observed BL asset wait sum = 73969 ms

Reading this table

  • Pack/file fetch+decode — full/stream variants show the time this request waited for pack initialization. Range-stream variants show metadata wait plus file-region fetch wait. miss is the first initializer for a pack, pending means this asset arrived while another request was already initializing the same pack, and hit means metadata/decode was already available at request start.
  • Baseline asset fetch — time to fetch this single asset over the wire in baseline mode. Adjacent for direct comparison.
  • Extract — pack.extract(file), in-memory, sub-millisecond.
  • SW overhead — total − fetch − extract. Browser-side Service Worker response construction and marker-message overhead. No Playwright/CDP fulfill path is included.
  • TokenPack total — fetch + extract + overhead. The wall-clock time spent producing this asset response.
  • Green/red coloring compares real work (fetch + extract) vs baseline fetch — i.e., what TokenPack would cost without the harness tax. Green on the TokenPack side = real work was faster than the baseline fetch.
  • outside TP manifest — baseline fetched this URL, but it is outside the comparable manifest-handled URL set for this sampled phase. This is not a TokenPack miss.
  • TP did not request — baseline fetched this comparable manifest URL, but the TokenPack run did not request it in the sampled phase. A large cluster usually means the TP page diverged or failed before reaching that import path; an isolated row can also come from feature flags, lazy imports, version drift, or conditional app flow.
  • TP-only (not in BL) — TokenPack requested this URL but baseline never did. Different code path got executed (feature flag, A/B variant, error-recovery branch).

Column sums overstate wall-clock because requests run in parallel. Iteration durations are the real answer.

const packCache = new Map()

async function fetch(url) {
  const { packId, path } = manifest.lookup(url)
  const pack = await memo(packCache, packId, async () => {
    const response = await nativeFetch(packUrl(packId))
    return decodeStream(response.body)
  })

  return new Response(await pack.text(path))
}

Reading the totals

Start with Comparable request window. This is the closest asset-level wall-clock comparison because it collapses overlapping request waits into a union: TP 1046 ms, comparable baseline 4546 ms.

Do not read diagnostic sums as page duration. Values like TP 11828 ms or baseline 63557 ms are sums across many overlapping rows. They are useful for finding where work accumulated, but they are not directly comparable to the top-level load time.

TP work breakdown = sum of unique pack/file fetch work + per-asset extract + per-asset overhead across served-from-pack assets = 135 ms + 11492 ms + 201 ms = 11828 ms
Excluded duplicated waits: 4939 ms. Raw paused sum before excluding waits: 16767 ms.

TP effective asset sum = TP work breakdown + sum of baseline-fetch ms for assets TP fell through on
= 11828 ms + 0 ms (0 fall-throughs paid network cost) = 11828 ms

Comparable baseline diagnostic sum = baseline fetch sum for rows TP served = 63557 ms
All observed BL asset wait sum = 76339 ms

Reading this table

  • Pack/file fetch+decode — full/stream variants show the time this request waited for pack initialization. Range-stream variants show metadata wait plus file-region fetch wait. miss is the first initializer for a pack, pending means this asset arrived while another request was already initializing the same pack, and hit means metadata/decode was already available at request start.
  • Baseline asset fetch — time to fetch this single asset over the wire in baseline mode. Adjacent for direct comparison.
  • Extract — pack.extract(file), in-memory, sub-millisecond.
  • SW overhead — total − fetch − extract. Browser-side Service Worker response construction and marker-message overhead. No Playwright/CDP fulfill path is included.
  • TokenPack total — fetch + extract + overhead. The wall-clock time spent producing this asset response.
  • Green/red coloring compares real work (fetch + extract) vs baseline fetch — i.e., what TokenPack would cost without the harness tax. Green on the TokenPack side = real work was faster than the baseline fetch.
  • outside TP manifest — baseline fetched this URL, but it is outside the comparable manifest-handled URL set for this sampled phase. This is not a TokenPack miss.
  • TP did not request — baseline fetched this comparable manifest URL, but the TokenPack run did not request it in the sampled phase. A large cluster usually means the TP page diverged or failed before reaching that import path; an isolated row can also come from feature flags, lazy imports, version drift, or conditional app flow.
  • TP-only (not in BL) — TokenPack requested this URL but baseline never did. Different code path got executed (feature flag, A/B variant, error-recovery branch).

Column sums overstate wall-clock because requests run in parallel. Iteration durations are the real answer.

Reading the totals

Start with Comparable request window. This is the closest asset-level wall-clock comparison because it collapses overlapping request waits into a union: TP 476 ms, comparable baseline 5330 ms.

Do not read diagnostic sums as page duration. Values like TP 475 ms or baseline 50060 ms are sums across many overlapping rows. They are useful for finding where work accumulated, but they are not directly comparable to the top-level load time.

TP work breakdown = sum of unique pack/file fetch work + per-asset extract + per-asset overhead across served-from-pack assets = 0 ms + 474 ms + 1 ms = 475 ms
Excluded duplicated waits: 1 ms. Raw paused sum before excluding waits: 476 ms.

TP effective asset sum = TP work breakdown + sum of baseline-fetch ms for assets TP fell through on
= 475 ms + 0 ms (0 fall-throughs paid network cost) = 475 ms

Comparable baseline diagnostic sum = baseline fetch sum for rows TP served = 50060 ms
All observed BL asset wait sum = 73969 ms

Reading this table

  • Pack/file fetch+decode — full/stream variants show the time this request waited for pack initialization. Range-stream variants show metadata wait plus file-region fetch wait. miss is the first initializer for a pack, pending means this asset arrived while another request was already initializing the same pack, and hit means metadata/decode was already available at request start.
  • Baseline asset fetch — time to fetch this single asset over the wire in baseline mode. Adjacent for direct comparison.
  • Extract — pack.extract(file), in-memory, sub-millisecond.
  • SW overhead — total − fetch − extract. Browser-side Service Worker response construction and marker-message overhead. No Playwright/CDP fulfill path is included.
  • TokenPack total — fetch + extract + overhead. The wall-clock time spent producing this asset response.
  • Green/red coloring compares real work (fetch + extract) vs baseline fetch — i.e., what TokenPack would cost without the harness tax. Green on the TokenPack side = real work was faster than the baseline fetch.
  • outside TP manifest — baseline fetched this URL, but it is outside the comparable manifest-handled URL set for this sampled phase. This is not a TokenPack miss.
  • TP did not request — baseline fetched this comparable manifest URL, but the TokenPack run did not request it in the sampled phase. A large cluster usually means the TP page diverged or failed before reaching that import path; an isolated row can also come from feature flags, lazy imports, version drift, or conditional app flow.
  • TP-only (not in BL) — TokenPack requested this URL but baseline never did. Different code path got executed (feature flag, A/B variant, error-recovery branch).

Column sums overstate wall-clock because requests run in parallel. Iteration durations are the real answer.

const packCache = new Map()
const fileCache = new Map()

async function fetch(url) {
  const { packId, path } = manifest.lookup(url)
  const remote = await memo(packCache, packId, () => fetchPackManifest(packUrl(packId)))

  return new Response(await memo(fileCache, url, async () => {
    const bytes = await fetchPackFile(remote, path) // buffered Range
    return text(decompress(bytes))
  }))
}

Reading the totals

Start with Comparable request window. This is the closest asset-level wall-clock comparison because it collapses overlapping request waits into a union: TP 1306 ms, comparable baseline 4546 ms.

Do not read diagnostic sums as page duration. Values like TP 32 ms or baseline 63557 ms are sums across many overlapping rows. They are useful for finding where work accumulated, but they are not directly comparable to the top-level load time.

TP work breakdown = sum of unique pack/file fetch work + per-asset extract + per-asset overhead across served-from-pack assets = 30 ms + 0 ms + 2 ms = 32 ms
Excluded duplicated waits: 11718 ms. Raw paused sum before excluding waits: 11750 ms.

TP effective asset sum = TP work breakdown + sum of baseline-fetch ms for assets TP fell through on
= 32 ms + 0 ms (0 fall-throughs paid network cost) = 32 ms

Comparable baseline diagnostic sum = baseline fetch sum for rows TP served = 63557 ms
All observed BL asset wait sum = 76339 ms

Reading this table

  • Pack/file fetch+decode — full/stream variants show the time this request waited for pack initialization. Range-stream variants show metadata wait plus file-region fetch wait. miss is the first initializer for a pack, pending means this asset arrived while another request was already initializing the same pack, and hit means metadata/decode was already available at request start.
  • Baseline asset fetch — time to fetch this single asset over the wire in baseline mode. Adjacent for direct comparison.
  • Extract — pack.extract(file), in-memory, sub-millisecond.
  • SW overhead — total − fetch − extract. Browser-side Service Worker response construction and marker-message overhead. No Playwright/CDP fulfill path is included.
  • TokenPack total — fetch + extract + overhead. The wall-clock time spent producing this asset response.
  • Green/red coloring compares real work (fetch + extract) vs baseline fetch — i.e., what TokenPack would cost without the harness tax. Green on the TokenPack side = real work was faster than the baseline fetch.
  • outside TP manifest — baseline fetched this URL, but it is outside the comparable manifest-handled URL set for this sampled phase. This is not a TokenPack miss.
  • TP did not request — baseline fetched this comparable manifest URL, but the TokenPack run did not request it in the sampled phase. A large cluster usually means the TP page diverged or failed before reaching that import path; an isolated row can also come from feature flags, lazy imports, version drift, or conditional app flow.
  • TP-only (not in BL) — TokenPack requested this URL but baseline never did. Different code path got executed (feature flag, A/B variant, error-recovery branch).

Column sums overstate wall-clock because requests run in parallel. Iteration durations are the real answer.

Reading the totals

Start with Comparable request window. This is the closest asset-level wall-clock comparison because it collapses overlapping request waits into a union: TP 2 ms, comparable baseline 5330 ms.

Do not read diagnostic sums as page duration. Values like TP 1 ms or baseline 50060 ms are sums across many overlapping rows. They are useful for finding where work accumulated, but they are not directly comparable to the top-level load time.

TP work breakdown = sum of unique pack/file fetch work + per-asset extract + per-asset overhead across served-from-pack assets = 0 ms + 0 ms + 1 ms = 1 ms
Excluded duplicated waits: 1 ms. Raw paused sum before excluding waits: 2 ms.

TP effective asset sum = TP work breakdown + sum of baseline-fetch ms for assets TP fell through on
= 1 ms + 0 ms (0 fall-throughs paid network cost) = 1 ms

Comparable baseline diagnostic sum = baseline fetch sum for rows TP served = 50060 ms
All observed BL asset wait sum = 73969 ms

Reading this table

  • Pack/file fetch+decode — full/stream variants show the time this request waited for pack initialization. Range-stream variants show metadata wait plus file-region fetch wait. miss is the first initializer for a pack, pending means this asset arrived while another request was already initializing the same pack, and hit means metadata/decode was already available at request start.
  • Baseline asset fetch — time to fetch this single asset over the wire in baseline mode. Adjacent for direct comparison.
  • Extract — pack.extract(file), in-memory, sub-millisecond.
  • SW overhead — total − fetch − extract. Browser-side Service Worker response construction and marker-message overhead. No Playwright/CDP fulfill path is included.
  • TokenPack total — fetch + extract + overhead. The wall-clock time spent producing this asset response.
  • Green/red coloring compares real work (fetch + extract) vs baseline fetch — i.e., what TokenPack would cost without the harness tax. Green on the TokenPack side = real work was faster than the baseline fetch.
  • outside TP manifest — baseline fetched this URL, but it is outside the comparable manifest-handled URL set for this sampled phase. This is not a TokenPack miss.
  • TP did not request — baseline fetched this comparable manifest URL, but the TokenPack run did not request it in the sampled phase. A large cluster usually means the TP page diverged or failed before reaching that import path; an isolated row can also come from feature flags, lazy imports, version drift, or conditional app flow.
  • TP-only (not in BL) — TokenPack requested this URL but baseline never did. Different code path got executed (feature flag, A/B variant, error-recovery branch).

Column sums overstate wall-clock because requests run in parallel. Iteration durations are the real answer.

const packCache = new Map()
const fileCache = new Map()

async function fetch(url) {
  const { packId, path } = manifest.lookup(url)
  const remote = await memo(packCache, packId, () => fetchPackManifest(packUrl(packId)))

  return new Response(await memo(fileCache, url, async () => {
    const file = await fetchPackFileStream(remote, path) // streaming Range
    return text(await readStream(file.stream))
  }))
}

Reading the totals

Start with Comparable request window. This is the closest asset-level wall-clock comparison because it collapses overlapping request waits into a union: TP 1332 ms, comparable baseline 4546 ms.

Do not read diagnostic sums as page duration. Values like TP 32 ms or baseline 63557 ms are sums across many overlapping rows. They are useful for finding where work accumulated, but they are not directly comparable to the top-level load time.

TP work breakdown = sum of unique pack/file fetch work + per-asset extract + per-asset overhead across served-from-pack assets = 26 ms + 0 ms + 6 ms = 32 ms
Excluded duplicated waits: 12821 ms. Raw paused sum before excluding waits: 12852 ms.

TP effective asset sum = TP work breakdown + sum of baseline-fetch ms for assets TP fell through on
= 32 ms + 0 ms (0 fall-throughs paid network cost) = 32 ms

Comparable baseline diagnostic sum = baseline fetch sum for rows TP served = 63557 ms
All observed BL asset wait sum = 76339 ms

Reading this table

  • Pack/file fetch+decode — full/stream variants show the time this request waited for pack initialization. Range-stream variants show metadata wait plus file-region fetch wait. miss is the first initializer for a pack, pending means this asset arrived while another request was already initializing the same pack, and hit means metadata/decode was already available at request start.
  • Baseline asset fetch — time to fetch this single asset over the wire in baseline mode. Adjacent for direct comparison.
  • Extract — pack.extract(file), in-memory, sub-millisecond.
  • SW overhead — total − fetch − extract. Browser-side Service Worker response construction and marker-message overhead. No Playwright/CDP fulfill path is included.
  • TokenPack total — fetch + extract + overhead. The wall-clock time spent producing this asset response.
  • Green/red coloring compares real work (fetch + extract) vs baseline fetch — i.e., what TokenPack would cost without the harness tax. Green on the TokenPack side = real work was faster than the baseline fetch.
  • outside TP manifest — baseline fetched this URL, but it is outside the comparable manifest-handled URL set for this sampled phase. This is not a TokenPack miss.
  • TP did not request — baseline fetched this comparable manifest URL, but the TokenPack run did not request it in the sampled phase. A large cluster usually means the TP page diverged or failed before reaching that import path; an isolated row can also come from feature flags, lazy imports, version drift, or conditional app flow.
  • TP-only (not in BL) — TokenPack requested this URL but baseline never did. Different code path got executed (feature flag, A/B variant, error-recovery branch).

Column sums overstate wall-clock because requests run in parallel. Iteration durations are the real answer.

Reading the totals

Start with Comparable request window. This is the closest asset-level wall-clock comparison because it collapses overlapping request waits into a union: TP 3 ms, comparable baseline 5330 ms.

Do not read diagnostic sums as page duration. Values like TP 1 ms or baseline 50060 ms are sums across many overlapping rows. They are useful for finding where work accumulated, but they are not directly comparable to the top-level load time.

TP work breakdown = sum of unique pack/file fetch work + per-asset extract + per-asset overhead across served-from-pack assets = 0 ms + 0 ms + 1 ms = 1 ms
Excluded duplicated waits: 2 ms. Raw paused sum before excluding waits: 3 ms.

TP effective asset sum = TP work breakdown + sum of baseline-fetch ms for assets TP fell through on
= 1 ms + 0 ms (0 fall-throughs paid network cost) = 1 ms

Comparable baseline diagnostic sum = baseline fetch sum for rows TP served = 50060 ms
All observed BL asset wait sum = 73969 ms

Reading this table

  • Pack/file fetch+decode — full/stream variants show the time this request waited for pack initialization. Range-stream variants show metadata wait plus file-region fetch wait. miss is the first initializer for a pack, pending means this asset arrived while another request was already initializing the same pack, and hit means metadata/decode was already available at request start.
  • Baseline asset fetch — time to fetch this single asset over the wire in baseline mode. Adjacent for direct comparison.
  • Extract — pack.extract(file), in-memory, sub-millisecond.
  • SW overhead — total − fetch − extract. Browser-side Service Worker response construction and marker-message overhead. No Playwright/CDP fulfill path is included.
  • TokenPack total — fetch + extract + overhead. The wall-clock time spent producing this asset response.
  • Green/red coloring compares real work (fetch + extract) vs baseline fetch — i.e., what TokenPack would cost without the harness tax. Green on the TokenPack side = real work was faster than the baseline fetch.
  • outside TP manifest — baseline fetched this URL, but it is outside the comparable manifest-handled URL set for this sampled phase. This is not a TokenPack miss.
  • TP did not request — baseline fetched this comparable manifest URL, but the TokenPack run did not request it in the sampled phase. A large cluster usually means the TP page diverged or failed before reaching that import path; an isolated row can also come from feature flags, lazy imports, version drift, or conditional app flow.
  • TP-only (not in BL) — TokenPack requested this URL but baseline never did. Different code path got executed (feature flag, A/B variant, error-recovery branch).

Column sums overstate wall-clock because requests run in parallel. Iteration durations are the real answer.

const packCache = new Map()
const fileCache = new Map()

async function fetch(url) {
  const { packId, path } = manifest.lookup(url)
  const remote = await memo(packCache, packId, () => fetchPackManifest(packUrl(packId)))

  if (!started(packId)) {
    const allFiles = fetchPackFilesCompressed(remote, remote.allPaths()) // buffered Ranges
    createLazyFilePromises(fileCache, allFiles)
    materializeRemainingFilesInRaf(fileCache)
  }

  return new Response(await fileCache.get(path)) // resolves when this file is ready
}

Do not read diagnostic sums as page duration. Values like TP 6910 ms or baseline 63557 ms are sums across many overlapping rows. They are useful for finding where work accumulated, but they are not directly comparable to the top-level load time.

TP work breakdown = sum of unique pack/file fetch work + per-asset extract + per-asset overhead across served-from-pack assets = 1011 ms + 0 ms + 5898 ms = 6910 ms
Excluded duplicated waits: 38980 ms. Raw paused sum before excluding waits: 45889 ms.

TP effective asset sum = TP work breakdown + sum of baseline-fetch ms for assets TP fell through on
= 6910 ms + 0 ms (0 fall-throughs paid network cost) = 6910 ms

Comparable baseline diagnostic sum = baseline fetch sum for rows TP served = 63557 ms
All observed BL asset wait sum = 76339 ms

Reading this table

  • Pack/file fetch+decode — full/stream variants show the time this request waited for pack initialization. Range-stream variants show metadata wait plus file-region fetch wait. miss is the first initializer for a pack, pending means this asset arrived while another request was already initializing the same pack, and hit means metadata/decode was already available at request start.
  • Baseline asset fetch — time to fetch this single asset over the wire in baseline mode. Adjacent for direct comparison.
  • Extract — pack.extract(file), in-memory, sub-millisecond.
  • SW overhead — total − fetch − extract. Browser-side Service Worker response construction and marker-message overhead. No Playwright/CDP fulfill path is included.
  • TokenPack total — fetch + extract + overhead. The wall-clock time spent producing this asset response.
  • Green/red coloring compares real work (fetch + extract) vs baseline fetch — i.e., what TokenPack would cost without the harness tax. Green on the TokenPack side = real work was faster than the baseline fetch.
  • outside TP manifest — baseline fetched this URL, but it is outside the comparable manifest-handled URL set for this sampled phase. This is not a TokenPack miss.
  • TP did not request — baseline fetched this comparable manifest URL, but the TokenPack run did not request it in the sampled phase. A large cluster usually means the TP page diverged or failed before reaching that import path; an isolated row can also come from feature flags, lazy imports, version drift, or conditional app flow.
  • TP-only (not in BL) — TokenPack requested this URL but baseline never did. Different code path got executed (feature flag, A/B variant, error-recovery branch).

Column sums overstate wall-clock because requests run in parallel. Iteration durations are the real answer.

Reading the totals

Start with Comparable request window. This is the closest asset-level wall-clock comparison because it collapses overlapping request waits into a union: TP 1 ms, comparable baseline 5330 ms.

Do not read diagnostic sums as page duration. Values like TP 1 ms or baseline 50060 ms are sums across many overlapping rows. They are useful for finding where work accumulated, but they are not directly comparable to the top-level load time.

TP work breakdown = sum of unique pack/file fetch work + per-asset extract + per-asset overhead across served-from-pack assets = 0 ms + 0 ms + 1 ms = 1 ms
Excluded duplicated waits: 1 ms. Raw paused sum before excluding waits: 1 ms.

TP effective asset sum = TP work breakdown + sum of baseline-fetch ms for assets TP fell through on
= 1 ms + 0 ms (0 fall-throughs paid network cost) = 1 ms

Comparable baseline diagnostic sum = baseline fetch sum for rows TP served = 50060 ms
All observed BL asset wait sum = 73969 ms

Reading this table

  • Pack/file fetch+decode — full/stream variants show the time this request waited for pack initialization. Range-stream variants show metadata wait plus file-region fetch wait. miss is the first initializer for a pack, pending means this asset arrived while another request was already initializing the same pack, and hit means metadata/decode was already available at request start.
  • Baseline asset fetch — time to fetch this single asset over the wire in baseline mode. Adjacent for direct comparison.
  • Extract — pack.extract(file), in-memory, sub-millisecond.
  • SW overhead — total − fetch − extract. Browser-side Service Worker response construction and marker-message overhead. No Playwright/CDP fulfill path is included.
  • TokenPack total — fetch + extract + overhead. The wall-clock time spent producing this asset response.
  • Green/red coloring compares real work (fetch + extract) vs baseline fetch — i.e., what TokenPack would cost without the harness tax. Green on the TokenPack side = real work was faster than the baseline fetch.
  • outside TP manifest — baseline fetched this URL, but it is outside the comparable manifest-handled URL set for this sampled phase. This is not a TokenPack miss.
  • TP did not request — baseline fetched this comparable manifest URL, but the TokenPack run did not request it in the sampled phase. A large cluster usually means the TP page diverged or failed before reaching that import path; an isolated row can also come from feature flags, lazy imports, version drift, or conditional app flow.
  • TP-only (not in BL) — TokenPack requested this URL but baseline never did. Different code path got executed (feature flag, A/B variant, error-recovery branch).

Column sums overstate wall-clock because requests run in parallel. Iteration durations are the real answer.

const packCache = new Map()
const fileCache = new Map()

async function fetch(url) {
  const { packId, path } = manifest.lookup(url)
  const remote = await memo(packCache, packId, () => fetchPackManifest(packUrl(packId)))

  if (!started(packId)) {
    const streams = fetchPackFilesStream(remote, remote.allPaths()) // streaming Ranges
    createFilePromises(fileCache, streams)
  }

  return new Response(await fileCache.get(path)) // each file resolves from its stream
}

Reading the totals

Start with Comparable request window. This is the closest asset-level wall-clock comparison because it collapses overlapping request waits into a union: TP 860 ms, comparable baseline 4546 ms.

Do not read diagnostic sums as page duration. Values like TP 192 ms or baseline 63557 ms are sums across many overlapping rows. They are useful for finding where work accumulated, but they are not directly comparable to the top-level load time.

TP work breakdown = sum of unique pack/file fetch work + per-asset extract + per-asset overhead across served-from-pack assets = 68 ms + 0 ms + 124 ms = 192 ms
Excluded duplicated waits: 5670 ms. Raw paused sum before excluding waits: 5861 ms.

TP effective asset sum = TP work breakdown + sum of baseline-fetch ms for assets TP fell through on
= 192 ms + 0 ms (0 fall-throughs paid network cost) = 192 ms

Comparable baseline diagnostic sum = baseline fetch sum for rows TP served = 63557 ms
All observed BL asset wait sum = 76339 ms

Reading this table

  • Pack/file fetch+decode — full/stream variants show the time this request waited for pack initialization. Range-stream variants show metadata wait plus file-region fetch wait. miss is the first initializer for a pack, pending means this asset arrived while another request was already initializing the same pack, and hit means metadata/decode was already available at request start.
  • Baseline asset fetch — time to fetch this single asset over the wire in baseline mode. Adjacent for direct comparison.
  • Extract — pack.extract(file), in-memory, sub-millisecond.
  • SW overhead — total − fetch − extract. Browser-side Service Worker response construction and marker-message overhead. No Playwright/CDP fulfill path is included.
  • TokenPack total — fetch + extract + overhead. The wall-clock time spent producing this asset response.
  • Green/red coloring compares real work (fetch + extract) vs baseline fetch — i.e., what TokenPack would cost without the harness tax. Green on the TokenPack side = real work was faster than the baseline fetch.
  • outside TP manifest — baseline fetched this URL, but it is outside the comparable manifest-handled URL set for this sampled phase. This is not a TokenPack miss.
  • TP did not request — baseline fetched this comparable manifest URL, but the TokenPack run did not request it in the sampled phase. A large cluster usually means the TP page diverged or failed before reaching that import path; an isolated row can also come from feature flags, lazy imports, version drift, or conditional app flow.
  • TP-only (not in BL) — TokenPack requested this URL but baseline never did. Different code path got executed (feature flag, A/B variant, error-recovery branch).

Column sums overstate wall-clock because requests run in parallel. Iteration durations are the real answer.

Reading the totals

Start with Comparable request window. This is the closest asset-level wall-clock comparison because it collapses overlapping request waits into a union: TP 2 ms, comparable baseline 5069 ms.

Do not read diagnostic sums as page duration. Values like TP 1 ms or baseline 49748 ms are sums across many overlapping rows. They are useful for finding where work accumulated, but they are not directly comparable to the top-level load time.

TP work breakdown = sum of unique pack/file fetch work + per-asset extract + per-asset overhead across served-from-pack assets = 0 ms + 0 ms + 1 ms = 1 ms
Excluded duplicated waits: 1 ms. Raw paused sum before excluding waits: 2 ms.

TP effective asset sum = TP work breakdown + sum of baseline-fetch ms for assets TP fell through on
= 1 ms + 0 ms (0 fall-throughs paid network cost) = 1 ms

Comparable baseline diagnostic sum = baseline fetch sum for rows TP served = 49748 ms
All observed BL asset wait sum = 73969 ms

Reading this table

  • Pack/file fetch+decode — full/stream variants show the time this request waited for pack initialization. Range-stream variants show metadata wait plus file-region fetch wait. miss is the first initializer for a pack, pending means this asset arrived while another request was already initializing the same pack, and hit means metadata/decode was already available at request start.
  • Baseline asset fetch — time to fetch this single asset over the wire in baseline mode. Adjacent for direct comparison.
  • Extract — pack.extract(file), in-memory, sub-millisecond.
  • SW overhead — total − fetch − extract. Browser-side Service Worker response construction and marker-message overhead. No Playwright/CDP fulfill path is included.
  • TokenPack total — fetch + extract + overhead. The wall-clock time spent producing this asset response.
  • Green/red coloring compares real work (fetch + extract) vs baseline fetch — i.e., what TokenPack would cost without the harness tax. Green on the TokenPack side = real work was faster than the baseline fetch.
  • outside TP manifest — baseline fetched this URL, but it is outside the comparable manifest-handled URL set for this sampled phase. This is not a TokenPack miss.
  • TP did not request — baseline fetched this comparable manifest URL, but the TokenPack run did not request it in the sampled phase. A large cluster usually means the TP page diverged or failed before reaching that import path; an isolated row can also come from feature flags, lazy imports, version drift, or conditional app flow.
  • TP-only (not in BL) — TokenPack requested this URL but baseline never did. Different code path got executed (feature flag, A/B variant, error-recovery branch).

Column sums overstate wall-clock because requests run in parallel. Iteration durations are the real answer.

Reading the totals

Start with Comparable request window. This is the closest asset-level wall-clock comparison because it collapses overlapping request waits into a union: TP 1311 ms, comparable baseline 4546 ms.

Do not read diagnostic sums as page duration. Values like TP 279 ms or baseline 63557 ms are sums across many overlapping rows. They are useful for finding where work accumulated, but they are not directly comparable to the top-level load time.

TP work breakdown = sum of unique pack/file fetch work + per-asset extract + per-asset overhead across served-from-pack assets = 47 ms + 0 ms + 232 ms = 279 ms
Excluded duplicated waits: 9656 ms. Raw paused sum before excluding waits: 9935 ms.

TP effective asset sum = TP work breakdown + sum of baseline-fetch ms for assets TP fell through on
= 279 ms + 0 ms (0 fall-throughs paid network cost) = 279 ms

Comparable baseline diagnostic sum = baseline fetch sum for rows TP served = 63557 ms
All observed BL asset wait sum = 76339 ms

Reading this table

  • Pack/file fetch+decode — full/stream variants show the time this request waited for pack initialization. Range-stream variants show metadata wait plus file-region fetch wait. miss is the first initializer for a pack, pending means this asset arrived while another request was already initializing the same pack, and hit means metadata/decode was already available at request start.
  • Baseline asset fetch — time to fetch this single asset over the wire in baseline mode. Adjacent for direct comparison.
  • Extract — pack.extract(file), in-memory, sub-millisecond.
  • SW overhead — total − fetch − extract. Browser-side Service Worker response construction and marker-message overhead. No Playwright/CDP fulfill path is included.
  • TokenPack total — fetch + extract + overhead. The wall-clock time spent producing this asset response.
  • Green/red coloring compares real work (fetch + extract) vs baseline fetch — i.e., what TokenPack would cost without the harness tax. Green on the TokenPack side = real work was faster than the baseline fetch.
  • outside TP manifest — baseline fetched this URL, but it is outside the comparable manifest-handled URL set for this sampled phase. This is not a TokenPack miss.
  • TP did not request — baseline fetched this comparable manifest URL, but the TokenPack run did not request it in the sampled phase. A large cluster usually means the TP page diverged or failed before reaching that import path; an isolated row can also come from feature flags, lazy imports, version drift, or conditional app flow.
  • TP-only (not in BL) — TokenPack requested this URL but baseline never did. Different code path got executed (feature flag, A/B variant, error-recovery branch).

Column sums overstate wall-clock because requests run in parallel. Iteration durations are the real answer.

Reading the totals

Start with Comparable request window. This is the closest asset-level wall-clock comparison because it collapses overlapping request waits into a union: TP 2 ms, comparable baseline 5330 ms.

Do not read diagnostic sums as page duration. Values like TP 1 ms or baseline 50060 ms are sums across many overlapping rows. They are useful for finding where work accumulated, but they are not directly comparable to the top-level load time.

TP work breakdown = sum of unique pack/file fetch work + per-asset extract + per-asset overhead across served-from-pack assets = 0 ms + 0 ms + 1 ms = 1 ms
Excluded duplicated waits: 2 ms. Raw paused sum before excluding waits: 2 ms.

TP effective asset sum = TP work breakdown + sum of baseline-fetch ms for assets TP fell through on
= 1 ms + 0 ms (0 fall-throughs paid network cost) = 1 ms

Comparable baseline diagnostic sum = baseline fetch sum for rows TP served = 50060 ms
All observed BL asset wait sum = 73969 ms

Reading this table

  • Pack/file fetch+decode — full/stream variants show the time this request waited for pack initialization. Range-stream variants show metadata wait plus file-region fetch wait. miss is the first initializer for a pack, pending means this asset arrived while another request was already initializing the same pack, and hit means metadata/decode was already available at request start.
  • Baseline asset fetch — time to fetch this single asset over the wire in baseline mode. Adjacent for direct comparison.
  • Extract — pack.extract(file), in-memory, sub-millisecond.
  • SW overhead — total − fetch − extract. Browser-side Service Worker response construction and marker-message overhead. No Playwright/CDP fulfill path is included.
  • TokenPack total — fetch + extract + overhead. The wall-clock time spent producing this asset response.
  • Green/red coloring compares real work (fetch + extract) vs baseline fetch — i.e., what TokenPack would cost without the harness tax. Green on the TokenPack side = real work was faster than the baseline fetch.
  • outside TP manifest — baseline fetched this URL, but it is outside the comparable manifest-handled URL set for this sampled phase. This is not a TokenPack miss.
  • TP did not request — baseline fetched this comparable manifest URL, but the TokenPack run did not request it in the sampled phase. A large cluster usually means the TP page diverged or failed before reaching that import path; an isolated row can also come from feature flags, lazy imports, version drift, or conditional app flow.
  • TP-only (not in BL) — TokenPack requested this URL but baseline never did. Different code path got executed (feature flag, A/B variant, error-recovery branch).

Column sums overstate wall-clock because requests run in parallel. Iteration durations are the real answer.
